An office-sized photocopier whirrs to life in the corner of Dave Morris’s living room in his council house in Tottenham, north London. “As you can see, lots of documents need to be copied,” he gestures to the dozens of stacked ring binders that fill up the floor in front of the fireplace, each one meticulously labelled and organised. “I’ve had about 12,000 documents so far,” he says. “Last time there were 40,000.”
If anyone needs a photocopier in their living room, it’s Morris. Along with his friend, Helen Steel, he was subject to libel action in 1990 from the fast-food giant McDonald’s after the environmental organisation he was part of, Greenpeace London, produced a flyer entitled “What’s wrong with McDonald’s?’ that made allegations about its practices on everything from child exploitation to rainforest destruction.
It was a David and Goliath battle that became the longest-running case in English legal history and was the subject of a BBC documentary in 2005. Morris, now 70, and Steel, 59, were denied legal aid or a jury, and they represented themselves for 313 days in court against a team of lawyers. A young up-and-coming socialist lawyer called Keir Starmer offered to give them free advice. After an appeal and a trip to the European Court of Human Rights, they won.
Thirty-four years after legal proceedings started, Steel and Morris are now heading back to court, and Morris’s photocopier is doing overtime once more. The “spy cops” inquiry is examining how, since 1968, about 140 officers from the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a branch of the Metropolitan Police, infiltrated around 1,000 campaign groups including the one run by the family of Stephen Lawrence and Greenpeace London.
SDS officers posing undercover as activists entered into fraudulent romantic relationships with women in order to feed back information to the police. Slowly women have come forward with details of how they were manipulated and abused, taking action against the Met. Mark Kennedy was the first to be exposed in 2010. He had sexual relationships with eight women.
The undercover policing, or spy cops inquiry, has already been plodding on for eight years, with lengthy delays. Last week the second of six “tranches” of the inquiry started, focusing on the activities of officers between 1982 and 1992. The inquiry has already cost the taxpayer an estimated £82 million.
“The police have spent £60 million defending the indefensible,” Morris says. “What the inquiry is showing is that these failures in the Met police go back decades.”
Steel, then a 23-year-old Greenpeace campaigner, had a two-year relationship with SDS officer John Dines, posing as John Barker. He had a wife and children. Her book, Deep Deception, details her experience.
“Helen was utterly traumatised,” Morris says. “He faked a mental breakdown and disappeared. There was no trace of him. Then she discovered that he used the identity of a deceased child. He made a beeline for Helen because he thought that she was involved with lots of protests and demonstrations. So he used her partly as cover but also for so-called intelligence.”
After years of searching, Steel tracked Dines down to Australia. In 2016, 24 years after she last saw him, she confronted him at an airport. “She is finding the inquiry very traumatic,” Morris says. Dines, now living in Australia, has given a confidential statement to the inquiry but has refused to give live evidence.
As well as being emotionally traumatic for Morris and particularly Steel, it has also emerged that Bob Lambert, one of the co-authors of the McDonald’s flyer, the document that provoked McDonald’s to bring the libel case, was another SDS officer. Lambert had at least four sexual relationships while undercover and fathered a child with an activist while having a wife and children who knew nothing of his double life.
Had it been known that a Met officer had been partly responsible for the flyer, the case may never have made it to court.
SDS officers were sharing information with McDonald’s throughout the McLibel trial. McDonald’s UK vice-president (formerly the Met’s chief superintendent in Brixton) employed spies to infiltrate Greenpeace London, and on two occasions these spies met up with SDS officers to share information.
“You can see that there’s a tangled web of subterfuge and collaboration between the SDS and McDonald’s,” Morris says.
Morris and Steel were awarded £10,000 in compensation in 2000 after suing the Met for disclosing their confidential information to McDonald’s. After finding out the Met withheld certain documents relating to the SDS, Morris is considering further legal action.
The inquiry made headlines last week when it was revealed that in his undercover position as Steel’s boyfriend, Dines was able to obtain privileged legal counsel given by Keir Starmer. Morris quoted Dines’s witness statement as saying: “I was ‘by the side’ of Helen Steel and Dave Morris in 1991 and relaying the legal advice back to my bosses in the SDS’”
Morris says Starmer “should be outraged” that his legal advice was fed from the Met to McDonald’s. “[He] had to put in years of unpaid and intense work to help defend the action.”
He recalls that during the McLibel saga he found the young Starmer “very easy to get on with, very helpful, very focused”. When everyone was telling the pair that they had no hope of winning, Keir basically said, ‘Let’s get a case together’.”
The McLibel case was one which helped to make Starmer’s name and propel him to become director of public prosecutions. Over the years, Morris has watched as the young socialist lawyer who helped him over the course of 15 years steadily manoeuvre his way to the top of the UK government.
“Keir Starmer chose his course,” Morris says. “It’s difficult commenting on where he is now. Gaining and wielding power changes people. Sometimes people start off idealistic and think ‘I can change things if I become prime minister’. But in fact, they’re the ones that get changed by that system.”
Is he still in touch with Starmer? “I won’t answer that,” Morris replies. Did he vote for him? “I don’t think I’ll answer that either”.
When Suella Braverman was home secretary she set an end date for the inquiry of 2026, but Morris is worried that it may end up being rushed, with much of the evidence yet to be heard. “We’ve said that the inquiry has to be conducted fairly.” This phase of the inquiry he says is the most important: “All the most scandalous stuff is coming out.”
The fight against McDonald’s has taken up half of Morris’s life. He was an unemployed single father during the trial and is now chairman of the National Federation of Parks and Green Spaces.
The walls of his living room are papered with crayon and paint stick-men drawings from his children, aged eight and ten, who live with their mother in Cornwall. He has an older son, Charlie, now 35, whose childhood he admits he largely missed because he was working 12 hours a day on the case in the 1990s.
Would he do it all again? He doesn’t miss a beat. “Yeah. I found the McLibel case very empowering,” he says. “We were able to put McDonalds on trial.”
